**Chapter 15**

The Eighth Server

*If one of eight servers is different, who would notice?*

Knight Capital Americas LLC was a U.S. broker-dealer. Its trading “generally represented approximately ten percent of all trading in listed U.S. equity securities” (¶11). Its automated order router was called SMARS.

SMARS had an old feature called Power Peg. “In 2003, Knight ceased using the Power Peg functionality” (¶14). But “in 2003, Knight elected to leave the Power Peg code on SMARS's production servers” (¶41). In Power Peg, “a cumulative quantity function counted the number of shares of the parent order that had been executed” (¶14). “In 2005, Knight moved the tracking of cumulative shares function”, and “Knight did not retest the Power Peg code after moving the cumulative quantity function” (¶14).

In 2012, Knight built new code for the New York Stock Exchange's Retail Liquidity Program, known as RLP, “which was scheduled to commence on August 1, 2012” (¶12). Knight “intended to delete the Power Peg code” (¶13), but it remained callable. And “The new RLP code also repurposed a flag that was formerly used to activate the Power Peg code” (¶13).

“Beginning on July 27, 2012, Knight deployed the new RLP code in SMARS in stages” (¶15). But “one of Knight's technicians did not copy the new code to one of the eight SMARS computer servers. Knight did not have a second technician review this deployment” (¶15). And “Knight had no written procedures that required such a review” (¶15).

On August 1, 2012, warnings appeared before trading began. From “approximately 8:01 a.m. ET”, automated emails “referenced SMARS and identified an error described as 'Power Peg disabled.'” (¶19). “Knight's system sent 97 of these e-mail messages to a group of Knight personnel before the 9:30 a.m. market open” (¶19). But “Knight personnel generally did not review them when they were received” (¶19). “These notifications were not acted upon before the market opened” (¶19).

At 9:30 a.m. the market opened. The SEC says the “orders sent with the repurposed flag to the eighth server triggered the defective Power Peg code” (¶16), and “this server continuously sent child orders, in rapid sequence, for each incoming parent order” (¶16).

“On the morning of August 1, the 33 Account began accumulating an unusually large position” (¶24). Knight had “assigned a $2 million gross position limit to the 33 Account” but had not linked it to automated controls (¶23). “At the opening of the market, senior Knight personnel observed a large volume of positions accruing in the 33 Account” (¶24).

Knight's main risk tool did not help. “Knight's primary risk monitoring tool, known as 'PMON,' is a post-execution position monitoring system” (¶25). “PMON relied entirely on human monitoring and did not generate automated alerts regarding the firm's financial exposure” (¶25). Knight also “did not have pre-set capital thresholds in the aggregate for the firm” (¶22).

There was no plan for this. “On August 1, Knight did not have supervisory procedures concerning incident response” (¶27). “Knight relied primarily on its technology team” (¶27). The team tried a rollback. “Knight uninstalled the new RLP code from the seven servers where it had been deployed correctly” (¶27). “This action worsened the problem” (¶27).

The damage, in the SEC's words: “For the 212 incoming parent orders that were processed by the defective Power Peg code”, SMARS produced “4 million executions in 154 stocks for more than 397 million shares in approximately 45 minutes” (¶17). Knight ended up with “an approximately $3.5 billion net long position in 80 stocks and an approximately $3.15 billion net short position in 74 stocks” (¶17). “Ultimately, Knight realized a $460 million loss on these positions” (¶17). Knight “experienced net capital problems” (¶10).

On October 16, 2013, the SEC issued its order. It found that Knight “willfully violated Section 15(c)(3) of the Exchange Act and Rule 15c3-5 thereunder” (¶49), known as the Market Access Rule. Knight was censured and ordered to “pay a civil money penalty in the amount of $12,000,000 ($12 million)”.

THE RECORD

- SEC Order, In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC, Release No. 70694, File No. 3-15570, October 16, 2013. Findings in numbered paragraphs. Sanctions in Section IV. [1]
- RLP code deployment to SMARS, beginning July 27, 2012. 8 servers, 1 missed. No second review. No written procedure (¶15). Deployment logs not published.
- Automated SMARS emails, August 1, 2012. 97 messages, from approximately 8:01 a.m. ET, before the 9:30 a.m. open. Sent to a group of Knight personnel. Text quoted: “Power Peg disabled” (¶19). Full text not published.
- PMON screens, August 1, 2012. Post-execution, human monitoring only, no automated alerts (¶25). Screens not published.
- 33 Account. A $2 million gross position limit, not linked to automated controls (¶23).
- Knight's written description of risk controls under Rule 15c3-5(b). The SEC found it “was incomplete” (¶29). Text not published.
- CEO certification under Rule 15c3-5(e). It “stated that Knight had in place 'processes' to comply with the rule” (¶34). Text not published.

THE CHAIN

1. Developers, 2003 and 2005. Left Power Peg on production servers and moved its counter without retesting it (¶14, ¶41). CONTROL POINT. The SEC says Knight “did not retest the Power Peg code”.
2. Developers, 2012. Reused the old Power Peg flag for RLP (¶13). The SEC says Knight had no “written protocol concerning the accessing of unused code” (¶26).
3. Deployment technician, from July 27, 2012. Copied the new code to 7 of 8 servers (¶15). CONTROL POINT. “Knight did not have a second technician review this deployment.”
4. Staff receiving the automated emails, 8:01 a.m. to 9:30 a.m., August 1. Did not act on 97 warnings (¶19). CONTROL POINT. “These notifications were not acted upon before the market opened.”
5. Risk controls. No firm-wide capital thresholds (¶22), a position limit not linked to automation (¶23) and a PMON tool with no alerts (¶25). CONTROL POINT. The SEC found Knight failed “to link pre-set capital thresholds to Knight's entry of orders” (¶37).
6. Technology team, during trading. Rolled back the good code on 7 servers (¶27). The SEC says “This action worsened the problem.”

WHAT THE RECORD RECOMMENDS

- The order required Knight to “Retain at its own expense one or more qualified independent consultants” to review its compliance with Rule 15c3-5 (¶51(A)).
- The SEC faulted Knight for having no guidance “as to when to disconnect a malfunctioning system from the market” (¶42), and for lacking controls “to prevent the entry of erroneous orders” (¶38).
- For a practitioner: require a second person or an automated check to confirm every server runs the same version after a deployment. Delete dead code instead of leaving it switched off. Send automated error alerts to a named owner, not only to a group inbox. Write down in advance who may pull a system off the market.

CAUTIONS

- The monitoring tool is called PMON. Do not call it PMES.
- The 97 emails were automated system messages, not warnings written by colleagues. The SEC says staff “generally did not review them”. It does not name who received them.
- The order does not say exactly when staff first understood the problem. It says senior personnel observed the positions “At the opening of the market” (¶24).
- The order does not mention a rescue or new financing. Say only that Knight had “net capital problems” (¶10).
- Do not name the technician. The SEC does not.
- The loss is “$460 million” (¶17), and ¶1 says “over $460 million”. Do not round up.
- The SEC order was read through a public mirror (Justia) because sec.gov could not be reached directly. Check paragraph numbers against the official PDF before publishing.

ELSEWHERE

- CrowdStrike, July 2024: an update went to every machine at once with no staged rollout (see Chapter 13). [2]
- Equifax, March 2017: a patch warning went to a large group and did not reach the system owner (see Chapter 14). [3]

FROM THE COURSE DECK

The SecureTree.ai CISSP deck, quoted exactly. Lessons may quote these lines and cite the slide.

- Slide 363: “Change management minimizes the risks associated with adding, modifying, or removing elements in IT systems.”
- Slide 363: “Review the Change: Verify the change was successful and within set parameters.”
- Slide 365: “Baseline Configuration: Establishes a standard set of configurations for systems.”
- Slide 122, Separation of Duties: “Prevents fraud, errors, and abuse by creating checks and balances.”
